title: Sunnah and hadith
hook: the sunnah is his way; hadith are the reports that carry it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hadith, and your line: a report. Said, did, or approved. Did you catch a "the Prophet said" somewhere, and ask which one it was? Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

A twig. A short stick from the arak tree, chewed at one end until it frays into a brush. It's called a miswak, and in mosques today you can still see someone pull one from a pocket before prayer. Why carry a twig? Because of a sentence in Sahih al-Bukhari. The Prophet said that if it would not be too hard on his community, he would have ordered them to use the miswak before every prayer. He didn't order it. He used it himself. So people still do. That twig is a small piece of something larger. Today, sunnah and hadith.
screen: `A TWIG FROM THE ARAK TREE.` → `HE WOULD HAVE ORDERED IT.` → `HE DIDN'T. HE USED IT.`

segments.voice: First, the two words. Sunnah is usually put into English as a way, a path, a habit of life. The Sunnah, capital S, is the way of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: how he prayed, ate, spoke, forgave, traded, slept. Hadith, as we met yesterday, are the reports. So the relation is simple to say. The sunnah is the way. Hadith are how the way is carried to people who never saw him. Second, why it matters. The Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation: "Verily in the messenger of Allah ye have a good example for him who looketh unto Allah and the Last Day, and remembereth Allah much." An example is something you watch. Hadith let later people watch. Third, not everything travels by written report alone. In Bukhari, the Prophet tells his companions: pray as you have seen me praying. The prayer was carried by people standing beside people, generation after generation. The Maliki school gives real weight to the living practice of the people of Medina, the city where he lived and died. Shia scholarship looks to the Imams of his family as trusted carriers and teachers of his way. Each, in its own terms, is asking: how does his way reach us? Fourth, a word that does two jobs. In the law, sunnah also names a recommended act, something rewarded but not required. That's why people speak of the sunnah prayers around the obligatory ones, or call the miswak a sunnah. So when someone says "it's sunnah", they may mean it's his way, or that it's recommended and not obligatory. Context tells you which. And sometimes it's a very small thing. Aisha reports, in Bukhari, that he liked to begin with the right: in putting on his sandals, in combing his hair, in washing for prayer, and in all his affairs.
screen: `THE WAY, AND THE REPORTS.` · `A GOOD EXAMPLE TO WATCH.` · `PRAY AS YOU'VE SEEN ME PRAY.` · `A RECOMMENDED ACT, TOO.`

segments.voice: The practice: choose one sunnah to live today. Settle, and breathe. Three small ones from these reports. Begin with the right as you put on your shoes. Clean your teeth with care before a prayer, or before a conversation that matters. Or help with the work at home before you leave it. Pick one. Then see it happen: the shoes, the sink, the doorway. If you're not Muslim, you can still try one as a way of understanding how Muslims live it, the way you'd try a recipe from a friend's grandmother. The bell holds the time.
Sunnah and hadith. The sunnah is the Prophet's way of life; hadith are the reports that carry it. Today's word.
Your line: the way, carried. Today, live the one sunnah you chose, once, and notice who first showed it to you, if anyone did. Tomorrow: chain and text. Day one thousand one hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims learn the sunnah from hadith, from teachers and from family practice, and keep small daily sunnahs such as starting with the right, using the miswak and praying the recommended sunnah prayers.
